title: movement applications (poster)
text:
A poster figure with 7 panels—split across 4 rows—showcasing movement application examples.
Rows 1–3 cover the elevated plus maze (EPM) dataset, whereas row 4 covers the rotating-mouse eye-tracking dataset:

title: movement applications (poster)
text:
Imports and style


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import sleap_io as sio
import xarray as xr

from movement import sample_data
from movement.filtering import (
    filter_by_confidence,
    interpolate_over_time,
    rolling_filter,
)
from movement.kinematics import compute_forward_vector_angle, compute_velocity
from movement.plots import plot_centroid_trajectory, plot_occupancy
from movement.roi import compute_region_occupancy, load_rois

from movement_figures import (
    add_inset_colorbar,
    apply_style,
    data_dir,
    figure_size,
    get_color,
    save_figure,
)

apply_style("poster")

title: movement applications (poster)
text:
Load and prepare data

EPM dataset
The EPM dataset ships with movement’s sample data. We apply a three-step cleaning pipeline (confidence filter, rolling median, linear gap interpolation) and keep both the raw and clean positions so we can compare them in the first panel.
We also compute the time fraction spent in each ROI and the head direction angle for the clean positions, which will be visualized in the third figure row.


Code
ds = sample_data.fetch_dataset(
    "DLC_single-mouse_EPM.predictions.h5", with_video=True
)
frame = plt.imread(ds.frame_path)
frame_h, frame_w = frame.shape[:2]

# Trajectory-panel background: the frame at the end of its time window.
video = sio.load_video(ds.video_path)
traj_end_sec = 250
traj_frame = video[int(traj_end_sec * ds.fps)]

pos_conf = filter_by_confidence(ds.position, ds.confidence, threshold=0.99)
pos_smooth = rolling_filter(pos_conf, window=9, statistic="median", min_periods=3)
pos_clean = interpolate_over_time(pos_smooth, method="linear", max_gap=5)

positions = xr.concat([ds.position, pos_clean], dim="data")
positions.coords["data"] = ["raw", "clean"]

rois = load_rois(data_dir() / "EPM_rois.geojson")

# The mouse is "in" an ROI only when both centre and tailbase are inside it.
roi_occ = compute_region_occupancy(pos_clean, rois)
mouse_in_roi = roi_occ.sel(
    keypoint=["centre", "tailbase"],
    individual="individual_0",
).all(dim="keypoint")

pct_time_in_roi = (
    mouse_in_roi.sum(dim="time") / mouse_in_roi.sizes["time"] * 100
)

# Radians, clockwise from the positive x-axis.
head_angle = compute_forward_vector_angle(
    pos_clean.sel(individual="individual_0"),
    left_keypoint="left_ear",
    right_keypoint="right_ear",
    reference_vector=(1, 0),
    camera_view="top_down",
    in_degrees=False,
)




Eye-tracking dataset
We use a dataset that’s already part of movement’s sample data and has been thoroughly explored in movement’s ‘Pupil tracking’ example. Here we extract the first video frame with tracked keypoints and the pupil centroid, as well as the pupil centroid’s horizontal velocity over a specific window (normalised by the mean eye position to remove head/camera motion).


Code
eye_ds = sample_data.fetch_dataset(
    "DLC_rotating-mouse_eye-tracking_stim-black.predictions.h5",
    with_video=True,
)
frame0 = sio.load_video(eye_ds.video_path)[0]

# Panel F
pos0 = eye_ds.position.isel(time=0).squeeze()
centroid0 = pos0.sel(keypoint=["pupil-L", "pupil-R"]).mean("keypoint")

# Panel G: relative to the eye midpoint, to remove head/camera motion.
eye_mid = eye_ds.position.sel(keypoint=["eye-L", "eye-R"]).mean("keypoint")
pos_norm = eye_ds.position - eye_mid
pupil_c = pos_norm.sel(keypoint=["pupil-L", "pupil-R"]).mean("keypoint")
velocity = compute_velocity(pupil_c)
vx = velocity.sel(space="x").squeeze().sel(time=slice(10, 25))

title: movement applications (poster)
text:
Build the figure


Code
fig = plt.figure(figsize=figure_size("double", height=17.5))
fig.get_layout_engine().set(hspace=0.06, wspace=0.08)
# One grid for all rows (no subgridspec) so constrained layout aligns edges.
# Columns split rows 2-3 in halves (5+3 | 8) and row 4 narrow/wide (5 | 3+8).
gs = fig.add_gridspec(4, 3, height_ratios=[2, 5, 5, 3], width_ratios=[5, 3, 8])

ax_trace = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :])
ax_traj  = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :2])
ax_heat  = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2])
ax_roi   = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, :2])
ax_polar = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, 2], projection="polar")
ax_frame = fig.add_subplot(gs[3, 0])
ax_vel   = fig.add_subplot(gs[3, 1:])

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel A: raw vs clean snout y-position                              #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
pos_sel = positions.sel(
    keypoint="snout",
    individual="individual_0",
    space="y",
    time=slice(240, 300),
)
pos_sel.sel(data="raw").plot.line(
    ax=ax_trace, color=get_color("orange", "Pastel2"), alpha=1.0,
    label="Raw snout position",
)
pos_sel.sel(data="clean").plot.line(
    ax=ax_trace, color=get_color("teal", "Set2"), alpha=1.0,
    label="Clean (after dropping outliers and smoothing)",
)
ax_trace.set_xlim(float(pos_sel.time.min()), float(pos_sel.time.max()))
ax_trace.set_title("")
ax_trace.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax_trace.set_ylabel("y position (px)")
# Legend in place of the title, clear of the data.
ax_trace.legend(
    loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0), frameon=True, framealpha=0.6, ncols=2
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel B: centroid trajectory                                        #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
ax_traj.imshow(traj_frame.mean(axis=2), cmap="gray")
plot_centroid_trajectory(
    pos_clean.sel(time=slice(traj_end_sec - 10, traj_end_sec)),
    individual="individual_0",
    keypoints=["centre", "tailbase", "left_ear", "right_ear"],
    ax=ax_traj,
    alpha=0.8,
    cmap="viridis",
)
add_inset_colorbar(ax_traj, "time (s)")
ax_traj.set_anchor("W")  # left-align the equal-aspect image with panel A
ax_traj.set_xlim(0, frame_w)
ax_traj.set_ylim(frame_h, 0)
ax_traj.set_title("Centroid trajectory")
ax_traj.axis("off")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel C: occupancy heatmap                                          #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
BIN_PIX = 30
bins = [
    np.arange(0, frame_w + BIN_PIX, BIN_PIX),
    np.arange(0, frame_h + BIN_PIX, BIN_PIX),
]

ax_heat.imshow(frame.mean(axis=2), cmap="gray")
_, ax_heat, _ = plot_occupancy(
    da=pos_clean,
    ax=ax_heat,
    alpha=0.8,
    bins=bins,
    cmin=10,
    norm="log",
    cmap="turbo",
)
add_inset_colorbar(ax_heat, "# frames")
ax_heat.set_xlim(0, frame_w)
ax_heat.set_ylim(frame_h, 0)
ax_heat.set_title("Occupancy heatmap")
ax_heat.axis("off")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel D: time in ROIs                                               #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
roi_colors = [
    get_color("teal", "Dark2") if roi.name.startswith("open")
    else get_color("pink", "Dark2") for roi in rois
]

ax_roi.imshow(frame.mean(axis=2), cmap="gray")
for i, roi in enumerate(rois):
    roi.plot(
        ax=ax_roi,
        edgecolor=roi_colors[i],
        facecolor="none",
    )
    cx, cy = roi.region.centroid.x, roi.region.centroid.y
    ax_roi.text(
        cx, cy,
        f"{float(pct_time_in_roi[i]):.0f}%",
        color=roi_colors[i],
        ha="center",
        va="center",
        fontsize="small",
    )
ax_roi.set_xlim(0, frame_w)
ax_roi.set_ylim(frame_h, 0)
ax_roi.set_title("Time spent in ROIs")
ax_roi.axis("off")
ax_roi.set_anchor("W")  # left-align with panel A

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel E: head direction polar histogram                             #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
BIN_WIDTH_DEG = 15
n_bins = int(360 / BIN_WIDTH_DEG)

head_angle.sel(time=slice(150, 300)).plot.hist(
    bins=np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, n_bins + 1),
    ax=ax_polar,
    density=True,
    color=get_color("teal", "Set2"),
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=1.0,
)
ax_polar.set_theta_direction(-1)   # clockwise
ax_polar.set_theta_offset(0)       # 0 deg at the right
ax_polar.set_xlabel("")
ax_polar.set_yticklabels([])

tick_angles = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 9)[:-1]
tick_labels_deg = list(range(0, 181, 45)) + list(range(0, -180, -45))[-1:0:-1]
ax_polar.set_xticks(tick_angles)
ax_polar.set_xticklabels([f"{t}\N{DEGREE SIGN}" for t in tick_labels_deg])
ax_polar.set_title("Head direction", pad=45)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel F: example eye frame with tracked keypoints + centroid        #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
ax_frame.imshow(frame0, cmap="gray")
ax_frame.scatter(
    pos0.sel(space="x"),
    pos0.sel(space="y"),
    s=120,
    color=get_color("teal", "Set2"),
)
ax_frame.scatter(
    centroid0.sel(space="x"),
    centroid0.sel(space="y"),
    s=120,
    color=get_color("orange", "Set2"),
)
ax_frame.invert_yaxis()  # the dataset was captured flipped

# Like axis("off"), but keeping the x/y labels.
ax_frame.set_xticks([])
ax_frame.set_yticks([])
for spine in ax_frame.spines.values():
    spine.set_visible(False)

ax_frame.set_xlabel("x")
ax_frame.set_ylabel("y")
ax_frame.set_anchor("W")  # left-align with panel A

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel G: pupil centroid x-velocity over time                        #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
vx.plot.line(
    ax=ax_vel, color=get_color("orange", "Set2"), label="Pupil centroid x velocity"
)
ax_vel.set_xlim(float(vx.time.min()), float(vx.time.max()))
ax_vel.set_title("Pupil centroid x velocity")
ax_vel.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax_vel.set_ylabel("velocity (px/s)");

title: README
text:
movement-figures makes reproducible figures and videos about the movement Python package, for papers, posters, talks, and social mediea. It produces two kinds of output:
Both build on the movement_figures Python package under src/, which holds the shared visual style (colours, fonts, plotting configurations) and reusable helpers, so all outputs look consistent.

title: README
text:
Setup
Requires uv. Clone the repo and install the environment:
git clone https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/movement-figures
cd movement-figures
uv sync                # if working on figures only
uv sync --extra video  # if working on videos too
Figures also need the Quarto CLI. Videos need a few more things, described under Videos.

title: README
text:
Figures
Each figure is a self-contained Quarto document (.qmd) under figures/. All figures share execution settings from figures/_metadata.yml, and are assembled into a gallery via index.qmd and _quarto.yml.
To render the gallery locally, run:
uv run quarto preview                  # live-reload while authoring one figure
uv run quarto render                   # build all figures + the gallery
The gallery is written to _site/; open _site/index.html in a browser to view it. Vector exports (pdf + svg) are written to outputs/ and committed; the gallery (_site/) and caches are not.

Data sources
Figures may draw on two data sources:

movement sample data: the primary source for most inputs, and the only option for large files (tracks, videos). Figures fetch these via movement.sample_data in their code cells, and each .qmd declares its datasets in Quarto frontmatter:
sample_data:
  - filename: DLC_single-mouse_EPM.predictions.h5
    with_video: true
The prefetch-sample-data helper reads these declarations and downloads everything up front, so a render finds the data already cached:
uv run prefetch-sample-data
The data/ folder in this repo: for small files only (< 500 KB), such as the ROI coordinates. This folder is git-tracked, so anything large would bloat the repo. Access it from a figure via movement_figures.data_dir().



Adding a figure

Copy an existing .qmd file in figures/.
Pick a target medium for apply_style: manuscript, poster, or presentation.
Adapt the .qmd frontmatter and code to fetch and process the data it needs and build the figure.
End with save_figure(fig, "<name>").
Run uv run quarto render and inspect the new files in outputs/, or the whole gallery in _site/index.html.

title: README
text:
Videos
Each video lives in its own folder under videos/, with its manim scenes and a video.yml describing how to build it. Building blocks shared between videos are in movement_figures.video.



Video
Description




videos/showcase
A silent ~2 min looping promo



Videos need manim, installed as the optional video extra, plus ffmpeg and pango/cairo on the system (e.g., on Ubuntu 24.04: sudo apt install ffmpeg libpango1.0-dev libcairo2-dev pkg-config):
uv sync --extra video
Each video needs files from its own assets/ folder (videos/<video>/assets), which is committed. Some inputs, such as third-party logos and large files, can’t be committed. You can put those in videos/<video>/inputs/ before rendering and declare them in the video’s video.yml manifest alongside any files you need to fetch from movement’s sample data.
The movement-video command checks the inputs and renders the video. For example, to render the showcase video:
uv run movement-video check videos/showcase    # are all inputs in place?
uv run movement-video render videos/showcase   # 720p draft
uv run movement-video render videos/showcase --resolution 1080p  # 1080p final
Renders are written to the video’s media/ folder, which isn’t committed. Finished versions are tagged and published as GitHub Releases. Each video’s own README explains its content, inputs and how to make a new version. For an example, see videos/showcase/README.md.

title: README
text:
Fonts
The fonts—Liberation Sans and Barlow are bundled under src/movement_figures/fonts/ and registered with matplotlib and manim automatically. Both are licensed under the SIL Open Font License; see the LICENSE-* files alongside them. The gallery and videos use them for all text, so figures and videos look consistent no matter what fonts are installed on your system.

title: README
text:
Development
Code quality is enforced with ruff (linting and formatting), codespell (spelling), and a set of pre-commit hooks.
Install the git hook once, so the checks run automatically on every commit:
uv run pre-commit install
After that, committing runs the hooks against your staged files. To run every hook across the whole repo on demand:
uv run pre-commit run --all-files
Generated figures under outputs/ are deliberatley excluded from the hooks so their committed vector files stay byte-stable across re-renders.

[!note] ruff only lints .py files—the Python inside figures/*.qmd code cells is not checked for now. Keep figure code tidy by hand, or factor reusable logic into src/movement_figures/ where it is linted.

Tests live in tests/ and run with uv run pytest; tests that need manim are skipped unless the video extra is installed.
Every pull request re-renders the site as a CI check that all figures still build, and every merge to main redeploys the gallery to GitHub Pages (see .github/workflows/render_and_deploy.yml). Videos are not rendered on CI, since their inputs aren’t all in the repo.

title: EPM occupancy (manuscript)
text:
Imports and style


Code
import sleap_io as sio
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from movement import sample_data
from movement.filtering import (
    filter_by_confidence, rolling_filter, interpolate_over_time
)
from movement.plots import plot_occupancy

from movement_figures import (
    add_inset_colorbar,
    apply_style,
    figure_size,
    napari_canvas_screenshot,
    save_figure,
)

apply_style("manuscript")

title: EPM occupancy (manuscript)
text:
Load and prepare data
We fetch the EPM sample dataset and apply a two-step cleaning pipeline: a confidence filter followed by a rolling median filter. We also (lazily) load the corresponding video.


Code
ds = sample_data.fetch_dataset(
    "DLC_single-mouse_EPM.predictions.h5", with_video=True
)
video = sio.load_video(ds.video_path)
n_frames, height, width, n_channels = video.shape
aspect_ratio = height / width

position_conf = filter_by_confidence(
    ds.position, ds.confidence, threshold=0.95
)
position_clean = rolling_filter(
    position_conf, window=5, statistic="median", min_periods=2
)

ds["position"] = position_clean


We grab a napari canvas screenshot of a single frame, with the tracked points and a short trailing track “tail”, mirroring what the movement GUI would show. The vide is loaded via the napari-video plugin, and the dataset’s points and tracks layers are added via the movement napari plugin.


Code
FRAME_SEC = 285  # time (s) of the snapshot; mouse is in an open arm here
TAIL_SEC = 1     # number of seconds to show in the trailing track tail
frame_index = int(FRAME_SEC * ds.fps)
tail_length = int(TAIL_SEC * ds.fps)

napari_frame = napari_canvas_screenshot(
    ds, ds.video_path,
    frame_index,
    tail_length=tail_length,
    zoom=True,
    display_text=True,
)


We also load a grayscale version of the same frame, which will be used as the background for the occupancy heatmap.


Code
frame = video[frame_index].mean(axis=2)  # grayscale

title: EPM occupancy (manuscript)
text:
Build the figure


Code
fig, (ax_napari, ax_heat) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=figure_size("double", aspect=aspect_ratio, ncols=2, extra=0)
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel A: napari canvas screenshot                                   #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
ax_napari.imshow(napari_frame)
ax_napari.set_title("Example video frame")
ax_napari.axis("off")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
# Panel B: occupancy heatmap                                          #
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
ax_heat.imshow(frame, cmap="gray")

# Bins of 30x30 pixels, covering the whole frame.
BIN_PIX = 30
bins = [
    np.arange(0, width + BIN_PIX, BIN_PIX),
    np.arange(0, height + BIN_PIX, BIN_PIX),
]

_, ax_heat, _ = plot_occupancy(
    da=position_clean,
    ax=ax_heat,
    bins=bins,
    alpha=0.8,
    cmin=10,  # hide bins with fewer than 10 frames
    norm="log",
)
add_inset_colorbar(ax_heat, "# frames")
ax_heat.set_xlim(0, width)
ax_heat.set_ylim(height, 0)
ax_heat.set_title("Occupancy heatmap")
ax_heat.axis("off")
